title: Lessons from Studying Every Memory System — Shlok Khemani, Independent

primary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk primarily focuses on memory systems, running profiles, context problems, and durable conversational state across consumer AI products. It examines consumer productivity assistants like ChatGPT and Claude while deriving cross-domain architectural lessons. The analysis reviews live production systems and their applied engineering tradeoffs in memory design. Requires familiarity with LLM context windows and memory concepts but remains accessible to AI engineers. It is a structured presentation delivered at an AI engineering conference. The findings are supported by specific reverse-engineered quantitative claims and direct transcript excerpts.

summary: Khemani's talk covers the evolution of consumer AI memory systems over roughly three years, with Part 1 tracing how ChatGPT and Claude independently developed their approaches and Part 2 distilling lessons. In 2023, ChatGPT maintained context only within single threads. ChatGPT memory v1 (Feb 2024) let users explicitly ask it to remember facts stored in a viewable, editable list, but this imposed management burden on users and suffered from staleness. ChatGPT v2 (April 2025) introduced a running profile—roughly 4,000 tokens across 16 sections of dense keyword clues—updated asynchronously every few days by scanning conversations. This removed user management burden but introduced a new problem: users couldn't view their raw profile (only via jailbreaking), and conflicts persisted, such as Khemani's profile claiming he visited both Thailand and Turkey with overlapping dates when he only went to Thailand. Claude's v1 (Aug 2025) took the opposite approach: no profile, just two tools for searching past conversations by keyword/topic or time period. After Khemani published a blog post calling Claude's architecture the opposite of ChatGPT's, Claude released v2 the same day, adding a 1,000-token running profile in full sentences, visible and editable in settings, refreshed every 24 hours. By mid-2025 both systems converged: each has a running profile plus retrieval tools over past conversations. Khemani's lessons span several themes. There is no single way to do memory—RAG was assumed but neither product uses it. Memory cannot be outsourced; all major consumer products build it in-house. Memory is a function of compute: maintaining a profile (update frequency and compute per update) and serving it (profile length in every context window) are competing costs, with ChatGPT choosing a large infrequently-updated profile and Claude choosing a small frequently-updated one. Continual learning is already here: the running profile loop—profile applied to conversations, new information synthesized back into the profile—constitutes continual learning outside the weights, though open questions remain about whether this will move into weights at an individual level and who pays for it. Finally, a fundamental context problem persists: memory is capped by how much context a system can gather about you. Khemani's Thailand/Turkey conflict illustrates this—the decision was made in person, evidence sat in his email, but ChatGPT didn't notice the conflict or try to resolve it. Each product builds its own isolated memory, none share with each other, and none can reason over rich existing context sources like email, calendar, and photos. He calls this a product problem, not a technology one.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: There is no single correct way to implement memory; ChatGPT and Claude evolved independently and converged on similar but not identical architectures.
Memory cannot be outsourced—it must be built alongside the product and evolve with it.
Memory is a function of compute: maintaining a profile (update frequency and compute per update) and serving it (profile length in every context window) are competing costs.
ChatGPT chose a large (4,000-token), less frequently updated profile; Claude chose a small (1,000-token), daily-updated profile—opposite tradeoffs on the same budget.
Continual learning already exists outside model weights via the running profile loop, but whether it will move into weights at an individual level remains an open question.
The context problem is unsolved: memory is capped by how much context a system can gather, and products cannot reason over rich sources like email, calendar, or photos.
Products build isolated, non-shared memories, forcing users to rebuild context from scratch in every product—Khemani calls this a product problem, not a technology one.
Staleness and conflict detection remain unsolved: ChatGPT didn't notice the Thailand/Turkey conflict or show curiosity about filling gaps, despite evidence in Khemani's email.
Neither ChatGPT nor Claude uses traditional RAG for memory despite that being the assumed approach.
Memory for AI is a three-year-old field, foundational to human-AI interaction, with much left to build.

sections.title: What memory means here and speaker background
sections.summary: Khemani scopes the talk to consumer personalization memory and introduces his year of reverse-engineering ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Poke memory systems, plus consulting work helping teams design memory.

sections.title: ChatGPT memory v1: the fact list
sections.summary: Before 2024, ChatGPT kept context only within a single thread. Memory v1 (Feb 2024) let users ask ChatGPT to remember facts, stored in a viewable, deletable list injected into every context window. Flaws: user bears management burden, and facts go stale.

sections.title: ChatGPT memory v2: the running profile
sections.summary: April 2025 brought a running profile updated asynchronously every few days by scanning conversations. Profile is ~4,000 tokens across 16 sections of dense keyword clues. Removes user management burden but raw profile is not viewable in settings (requires jailbreaking). Staleness persists: profile claims overlapping trips to Thailand and Turkey when only Thailand happened.

sections.title: Claude's memory: from tools to profile
sections.summary: Claude v1 (Aug 2025) had no profile—only two tools to search past conversations by keyword/topic or time period. On Sept 11, 2025, Khemani published that Claude's architecture was the opposite of ChatGPT's; Claude released v2 the same day with a 1,000-token, full-sentence, visible, editable profile updated every 24 hours.

sections.title: Convergence of ChatGPT and Claude memory
sections.summary: By mid-2025 both products converged: each has a running profile (visible and editable, somewhat), plus retrieval tools over past conversations. ChatGPT added a conversation retrieval tool and made the profile somewhat visible in June 2025, deprecating the v1 fact list.

sections.title: Lesson 1: No single way to do memory
sections.summary: RAG was assumed to be the way, but neither ChatGPT nor Claude uses it. They evolved independently with different approaches and still differ in implementation details. Gemini has timing logs per memory; agent systems use markdown files, heartbeats, knowledge bases. Memory cannot be outsourced—all top consumer products build it in-house.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Memory is a function of compute
sections.summary: Running profiles have two costs: maintenance (update frequency and compute per update) and serving (profile length in every context window). An ideal unconstrained system would update hourly with powerful sub-agents and store 400,000 tokens, but GPU constraints force tradeoffs. ChatGPT: 4,000 tokens, updated every few days. Claude: 1,000 tokens, updated every 24 hours.

sections.title: Continual learning is already here
sections.summary: The running profile loop—profile applied to conversations, new information synthesized back into the profile—constitutes continual learning outside the weights. Open questions remain: will each person get their own self-learning model, what data kicks off the process, and who pays? Khemani references Guan's essay 'Guardian Angels' on the future of one model per person.

sections.title: The context problem no architecture solves
sections.summary: Memory is capped by how much context a system can gather. The Thailand/Turkey conflict illustrates this: the decision was made in person, evidence sat in email as flight and hotel bookings, but ChatGPT didn't notice the conflict or try to resolve it. Even connected to email, ChatGPT doesn't reason over it. Khemani calls this a product problem, not a technology one—nothing in the system is curious about filling information gaps.

sections.title: Products that each know you separately
sections.summary: Khemani's personal stack—chatbots, assistants, vertical apps, agents, hardware—each builds its own isolated memory, none shared. Rich context sources like email, calendar, and photos go unreasoned over. He asks when personal AI will feel personal. Despite frustration, he notes memory for AI is a three-year-old field, foundational to human-AI interaction, with much left to build.
